## Project Survival Analysis exploration

Based on cds data base from the full study git.

## Data loading + packages

Load all needed packages.

```{r}
library(survival)
library(DESeq2)
library(GSVA)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggsurvfit)
library(ggpubr)
library(tidyverse)
library(survminer)
```

Set working directory, create output plot directory, and load the dataset.

```{r}
plot_dir <- "../results/plot"
dir.create(plot_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

clean_clinical_TMB <- readRDS("data/processed/clean_clinical_TMB.rds")
clean_clinical_TNB <- readRDS("data/processed/clean_clinical_TNB.rds")

glimpse(clean_clinical_TMB)
glimpse(clean_clinical_TNB)
```

### Helper functions

```{r}
# Convert a survdiff() chi-squared statistic to a p-value.
lr_p <- function(x) {
  pchisq(x$chisq, df = length(x$n) - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
}

# Draw a Kaplan–Meier curve with confidence bands, a risk table, and p-value.
km_plot <- function(fit, title, p) {
  ggsurvfit(fit, linewidth = 1) +
    add_confidence_interval() +
    annotate(
      "text",
      x = Inf, y = Inf,
      label = paste0(
        "Log-rank p = ",
        format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)
      ),
      hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.4
    ) +
    add_risktable(
      risktable_stats = c("n.risk", "cum.event"),
      stats_label = c("At risk", "Events")
    ) +
    scale_ggsurvfit() +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Overall survival (months)",
      y = "Overall survival probability",
      color = "Group",
      fill = "Group"
    ) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

## TMB Survival Analysis

Several variable to check : PD vs SD, R vs NR, IC level, TMB, TNB, TC level, ....

Begin by inspecting TMB distribution to find a good cut-off point.

```{r}
p_tmb_dist <- ggplot(
  clean_clinical_TMB,
  aes(x = FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB)
) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "TMB Distribution")

print(p_tmb_dist)

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(plot_dir, "distribution_TMB.png"),
  plot = p_tmb_dist,
  width = 7,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)
```

Looks like a Negative binomiale distribution, thus taking median value would create imbalanced groups.

```{r}
p_tmb_log_dist <- ggplot(
  clean_clinical_TMB,
  aes(x = log(FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB + 1))
) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "TMB Distribution")

print(p_tmb_log_dist)

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(plot_dir, "distribution_TMB_log.png"),
  plot = p_tmb_log_dist,
  width = 7,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)
```

### Whole cohort

```{r}
# Find the optimal cutpoint for TMB against overall survival
cut_tmb <- surv_cutpoint(
  data = clean_clinical_TMB,
  time = "os",
  event = "censOS",
  variables = "FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB",
  minprop = 0.1
)

summary(cut_tmb)

png(
  filename = file.path(plot_dir, "cutpoint_TMB.png"),
  width = 7,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  res = 300
)
plot(cut_tmb, "FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB", palette = "npg")
dev.off()

plot(cut_tmb, "FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB", palette = "npg")

# Categorize patients into High vs. Low TMB using the cutpoint
cat_tmb <- surv_categorize(cut_tmb)
```

```{r}
# Add the new factor column back to your clinical data frame
clean_clinical_TMB <- clean_clinical_TMB |>
  mutate(TMB_Cutpoint_Group = cat_tmb$FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB)

table(clean_clinical_TMB$TMB_Cutpoint_Group)

fit_tmb <- survfit(Surv(os, censOS) ~ TMB_Cutpoint_Group,
                   data = clean_clinical_TMB)
lr_tmb <- survdiff(Surv(os, censOS) ~ TMB_Cutpoint_Group,
                   data = clean_clinical_TMB)

p_km_tmb <- km_plot(
  fit_tmb,
  "Survival analysis stratified by TMB",
  lr_p(lr_tmb)
)

print(p_km_tmb)

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(plot_dir, "km_survival_TMB.png"),
  plot = p_km_tmb,
  width = 7,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)
```

### Hazard Ratio

```{r}
# Model TMB continuously; one unit is one doubling of TMB
cox_tmb <- coxph(
  Surv(os, censOS) ~ log2(FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB + 1),
  data = clean_clinical_TMB
)

# Display the hazard ratio and 95% confidence interval
exp(cbind(
  HR = coef(cox_tmb),
  confint(cox_tmb)
))
```

```{r}
# Display the complete Cox-model result
summary(cox_tmb)
```

```{r}
# Check the proportional-hazards assumption
ph_tmb <- cox.zph(cox_tmb)
ph_tmb
```

A continuous Cox proportional hazards model on $\log_2(\text{TMB} + 1)$ shows that higher Tumor Mutational Burden is significantly associated with a lower hazard of death for the whole cohort and therefore better overall survival ($\text{HR} = 0.75$, 95% CI: $0.64\text{-}0.88$). The proportional hazards assumption is not violated ($p = 0.38$), supporting a consistent protective association across follow-up time and reinforcing our Kaplan-Meier findings without relying on a single cutoff.

```{r}
# Model TMB continuously; one unit is one doubling of TMB
cox_tmb_r <- coxph(
  Surv(os, censOS) ~ log2(FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB + 1),
  data = df_r
)

# Display the hazard ratio and 95% confidence interval
exp(cbind(
  HR = coef(cox_tmb_r),
  confint(cox_tmb_r)
))
```

```{r}
cox.zph(cox_tmb_r)
```

```{r}
# Model TMB continuously; one unit is one doubling of TMB
cox_tmb_nr <- coxph(
  Surv(os, censOS) ~ log2(FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB + 1),
  data = df_nr
)

# Display the hazard ratio and 95% confidence interval
exp(cbind(
  HR = coef(cox_tmb_nr),
  confint(cox_tmb_nr)
))
```

```{r}
cox.zph(cox_tmb_nr)
```

However, when fitting the continuous Cox model separately within responders (`df_r`) and non-responders (`df_nr`), the 95% confidence intervals include $1$ in both subsets. This indicates no statistically significant continuous association between $\log_2(\text{TMB} + 1)$ and overall survival within either response group alone, likely reflecting the small sample sizes and event counts per subgroup (as well as reduced contrast once stratified by response status), and therefore warrants cautious, exploratory interpretation rather than a definitive within-group conclusion.

Within responders ($n = 61$: 50 high-TMB and 11 low-TMB), only 4 events occurred in total (2 per group), with the two events in the low-TMB group appearing earlier than the two events in the high-TMB group. Because event counts are so sparse - and the 95% CI already spans $1$ - the proportional hazards test (`cox.zph` $p = 0.038$) should be interpreted cautiously as a sign that the subgroup model is underpowered/unstable rather than a robust standalone finding.

```{r}
zph_tmb_r <- cox.zph(cox_tmb_r)

png(
  filename = file.path(plot_dir, "zph_TMB_responders.png"),
  width = 7,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  res = 300
)
plot(zph_tmb_r)
dev.off()

plot(zph_tmb_r)
```

### Hazard Ratio

```{r}
# Model TMB continuously; one unit is one doubling of TMB
cox_tnb <- coxph(
  Surv(os, censOS) ~ log2(Neoantigen.burden.per.MB + 1),
  data = clean_clinical_TNB
)

# Display the hazard ratio and 95% confidence interval
exp(cbind(
  HR = coef(cox_tnb),
  confint(cox_tnb)
))
```

```{r}
# Display the complete Cox-model result
summary(cox_tnb)
```

```{r}
# Check the proportional-hazards assumption
ph_tnb <- cox.zph(cox_tnb)
ph_tnb
```

A continuous Cox proportional hazards model on $\log_2(\text{TNB} + 1)$ shows that higher neoantigen burden is associated with a substantially lower hazard of death and better overall survival ($\text{HR} = 0.51$, 95% CI: $0.39\text{--}0.69$), with no violation of the proportional hazards assumption ($p = 0.53$). While this points to a stronger per-unit protective association than observed for $\log_2(\text{TMB} + 1)$ ($\text{HR} = 0.75$), direct comparison should keep in mind differences in scale/transformation and cohort subsets between the TMB and TNB analyses.

```{r}
# Model TMB continuously; one unit is one doubling of TMB
cox_tnb_r <- coxph(
  Surv(os, censOS) ~ log2(Neoantigen.burden.per.MB + 1),
  data = df_tnb_r
)

# Display the hazard ratio and 95% confidence interval
exp(cbind(
  HR = coef(cox_tnb_r),
  confint(cox_tnb_r)
))
```

```{r}
cox.zph(cox_tnb_r)
```

```{r}
# Model TMB continuously; one unit is one doubling of TMB
cox_tnb_nr <- coxph(
  Surv(os, censOS) ~ log2(Neoantigen.burden.per.MB + 1),
  data = df_tnb_nr
)

# Display the hazard ratio and 95% confidence interval
exp(cbind(
  HR = coef(cox_tnb_nr),
  confint(cox_tnb_nr)
))
```

```{r}
cox.zph(cox_tnb_nr)
```

The same pattern holds for neoantigen burden: when the continuous $\log_2(\text{TNB} + 1)$ Cox model is fit separately within responders and non-responders, the 95% confidence intervals again include $1$, underscoring that while overall survival benefits associate with higher burden across the cohort, smaller within-subgroup sample and event counts limit statistical precision within each response group alone.

## Shared Complete-Case Comparison (TMB vs. TNB)

Because `clean_clinical_TMB` and `clean_clinical_TNB` are filtered separately for missing values in each biomarker, their patient cohorts do not overlap completely. Here we isolate the shared complete-case subset with non-missing values for both `FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB` and `Neoantigen.burden.per.MB` (as well as survival outcome variables) so we can compare the two continuous Cox models on the exact same patients.

```{r}
# Identify shared patients using row names with non-missing survival data
common_ids <- intersect(
  rownames(clean_clinical_TMB),
  rownames(clean_clinical_TNB)
)

df_shared <- clean_clinical_TMB[common_ids, , drop = FALSE] |>
  mutate(Neoantigen.burden.per.MB = clean_clinical_TNB[common_ids, "Neoantigen.burden.per.MB"]) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB),
    !is.na(Neoantigen.burden.per.MB),
    !is.na(os),
    !is.na(censOS)
  )

cat("Shared complete-case sample size (n):", nrow(df_shared), "\n")
cat("Total OS events in shared subset:", sum(df_shared$censOS == 1, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
```

```{r}
# Continuous Cox model for TMB on the shared subset
cox_shared_tmb <- coxph(
  Surv(os, censOS) ~ log2(FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB + 1),
  data = df_shared
)

exp(cbind(
  HR = coef(cox_shared_tmb),
  confint(cox_shared_tmb)
))

cox.zph(cox_shared_tmb)
```

```{r}
# Continuous Cox model for TNB on the shared subset
cox_shared_tnb <- coxph(
  Surv(os, censOS) ~ log2(Neoantigen.burden.per.MB + 1),
  data = df_shared
)

exp(cbind(
  HR = coef(cox_shared_tnb),
  confint(cox_shared_tnb)
))
cox.zph(cox_shared_tnb)
```

Evaluating both continuous $\log_2(\text{burden} + 1)$ Cox models on the shared complete-case cohort removes differences in sample composition and event counts between the TMB and TNB analyses, allowing a more direct check of whether neoantigen burden shows a stronger protective association with overall survival than TMB on the same patients.

On the shared complete-case cohort, the protective association with overall survival persists for both $\log_2(\text{TNB} + 1)$ ($\text{HR} = 0.48$, 95% CI: $0.35\text{-}0.67$; `cox.zph` $p = 0.93$) and $\log_2(\text{TMB} + 1)$ ($\text{HR} = 0.73$, 95% CI: $0.61\text{-}0.87$; `cox.zph` $p = 0.34$). Because both models are evaluated on the exact same patients without violations of the proportional hazards assumption, this confirms that the stronger per-unit hazard reduction observed for neoantigen burden compared with TMB is not simply an artifact of differing sample subsets.

## Multivariable Cox Models Adjusting for Response

To test whether continuous $\log_2(\text{TMB} + 1)$ and $\log_2(\text{TNB} + 1)$ remain associated with overall survival after accounting for response status (`Responder_Group`), we fit multivariable Cox proportional hazards models without shrinking sample sizes by splitting into separate `R` and `NR` subsets.

```{r}
# Ensure Responder_Group is a factor with a clear reference level (e.g., NR as reference)
clean_clinical_TMB <- clean_clinical_TMB |>
  mutate(Responder_Group = factor(Responder_Group, levels = c("NR", "R")))

clean_clinical_TNB <- clean_clinical_TNB |>
  mutate(Responder_Group = factor(Responder_Group, levels = c("NR", "R")))

# Multivariable Cox model for TMB adjusted for responder status
cox_mv_tmb <- coxph(
  Surv(os, censOS) ~ log2(FMOne.mutation.burden.per.MB + 1) + Responder_Group,
  data = clean_clinical_TMB
)

exp(cbind(
  HR = coef(cox_mv_tmb),
  confint(cox_mv_tmb)
))
summary(cox_mv_tmb)
cox.zph(cox_mv_tmb)
```

```{r}
# Multivariable Cox model for TNB adjusted for responder status
cox_mv_tnb <- coxph(
  Surv(os, censOS) ~ log2(Neoantigen.burden.per.MB + 1) + Responder_Group,
  data = clean_clinical_TNB
)

exp(cbind(
  HR = coef(cox_mv_tnb),
  confint(cox_mv_tnb)
))

summary(cox_mv_tnb)
cox.zph(cox_mv_tnb)
```

In both multivariable models, `Responder_Group` is the dominant predictor of overall survival—with responders (`Responder_GroupR`) showing a markedly lower hazard of death than non-responders in both the TMB model ($\text{HR} = 0.037$, 95% CI: $0.014\text{-}0.102$) and the TNB model ($\text{HR} = 0.035$, 95% CI: $0.011\text{-}0.111$). Once adjusted for response status, the hazard ratios for $\log_2(\text{TMB} + 1)$ ($\text{HR} = 1.00$, 95% CI: $0.84\text{-}1.19$) and $\log_2(\text{TNB} + 1)$ ($\text{HR} = 0.85$, 95% CI: $0.64\text{-}1.12$) attenuate toward $1$ with confidence intervals crossing $1$, supporting a model in which higher burden improves survival largely through - or alongside - achieving a clinical response rather than exerting a large independent effect conditional on response group.
